Example

Borrow €10,000 for 12 months against BTC worth €20,000 (LTV 50%). Liquidated at LTV 80%.

45 of 100 simulated price paths end with this loan liquidated within 12 months.

A simulated price path is one possible course of the BTC price over your loan, built from real price moves since 2014, with recent years counting more. The page calculates 10,000 of them and counts what the lender would do in each. Example: 64 of 100 means that in 64 of every 100 paths, the loan was liquidated before it ended. It is not a forecast and not a promise.

Where to find these numbers

Your offer or loan agreement contains five numbers this page needs. Look for these words:

  1. Loan amount: "principal", "loan amount" (in German contracts: "Darlehensbetrag")
  2. Initial LTV: "LTV", "loan-to-value" (German: "Beleihungsquote"). If only the collateral amount is given: loan ÷ collateral value
  3. Liquidation LTV: "liquidation" (German: "Verwertung"), the section on selling or enforcing the collateral
  4. Duration: "term", "maturity" (German: "Laufzeit")
  5. Interest rate: "nominal rate", "interest rate" (German: "Sollzins"). Not the APR: the page calculates that itself

The other terms are in sections called "fees", "collateral monitoring" or "margin call". The page fills them with starting values you can change under "More terms from your offer".

LTV = loan ÷ value of the BTC you pledge. A lower LTV means more BTC behind the same loan, so the price can fall further. Example: loan €10,000 at 50% LTV means you pledge BTC worth €20,000. At a BTC price of €50,000 that is 0.4 BTC.
%

Some lenders count the interest for the whole term in the initial LTV. Then enter the BTC you pledge instead, and ask which amount their liquidation LTV refers to.

When BTC falls, your loan stays the same but your BTC is worth less, so the LTV rises. At this LTV the lender sells your BTC; in a fast fall, below this price. A higher number gives you more room. Example: €10,000 loan, 0.4 BTC, liquidation at 80%: the sale happens when 0.4 BTC is worth €12,500, which is a BTC price of €31,250.
%

If the price falls: your lender's rules and your planYour lender: Margin call at 70%: a warning only · At 80%: everything is sold · Fee 5% of the amount owed · Your plan: No top-ups
Margin call and sale
A margin call comes before a liquidation: your LTV has risen to a warning level. What happens next depends on your lender. It may be only a warning. You may have some hours to top up or repay part (the cure period), or the lender sells everything or just enough. Or the lender sells part of your BTC at once. Example: margin call at 70% with 48 hours to top up: if the LTV is still 70% after 48 hours, the lender sells.

When do you pay the interest?
If interest is added to the loan, what you owe grows every month, and so does the liquidation price. Example: €10,000 at 10% for a year. Paid monthly, you owe €10,000 all year. Added to the loan, you owe about €11,000 at the end, and the liquidation price rises by about 10%.

Before you sign: 8 questions to ask your lenderWhat happens after a margin call, which price counts, who holds your BTC …
  • At which LTV do you sell my BTC?
  • What exactly happens after a margin call? Only a warning, or a sale after a number of hours? Everything or only part?
  • Which BTC price do you use: one exchange, an average, over how long?
  • Do you sell all my BTC or only as much as needed?
  • What does a liquidation cost?
  • Who holds my BTC? Is it kept separate? Is it lent out?
  • If I switch lenders: how is my current loan paid off, and how long is my BTC in transit?
  • Is there a fee for repaying early?

At €41,039 (margin call): you get a warning. Topping up 0.1392 BTC (≈ €5,714) or repaying €2,857 would bring the LTV back to 50%.

At €35,909 (liquidation): the lender sells at least 0.2925 BTC, including the fee, and the loan ends.

If BTC falls through this price, this page counts the sale at the lowest price of the hour in which it is reached.

More than half of all liquidations in the simulation happen in the first 5 months.

20 possible price paths

The simulation takes the real daily price moves of BTC since 2014 and cuts them into 30-day pieces. It joins randomly chosen pieces into a new path for the length of your loan. Each path keeps the real mix of calm and wild weeks. Example: one path may start with a stretch from May 2021 (a 50% fall) followed by one from late 2023 (a steady rise).

Some ✕ sit above the red line: there, a margin call (amber line) was not fixed in time, or the lender sold part of the BTC.

    Cost including the liquidation risk

    Including the liquidation risk: about €2,120 (about 21.8% a year instead of 11.6%).

    €1,020 of it is the cost of the risk: what full protection against a liquidation would cost on average in the simulated price paths.

    Each forced sale is counted at the lowest price of the hour in which BTC reaches your liquidation price: in a fast fall, below it.

    It is not a fee anyone charges you. In 55 of 100 price paths it is zero; after a liquidation, it is far more. Use it to compare offers: lower interest with a higher liquidation chance can cost more in total.

    How this number is made →

    Borrow or sell?

    Borrowing only beats selling BTC today if BTC rises enough. Assuming you repay by selling BTC at the end:

    BTC must be at least 11.1% higher at the end, and the loan must not be liquidated on the way.

    What this does not include
    • The future can be wilder than the past. Every model can be wrong.
    • The lender itself could fail, freeze withdrawals or lose your BTC.
    • During an exchange outage, your lender may sell at prices this page never saw. You may then get back less.
    • Your lender may measure the BTC price differently from this page.

    Glossary
    LTV (loan-to-value)
    The loan divided by the value of the pledged BTC, in percent. Loan €10,000 and BTC worth €20,000 means an LTV of 50%. When the BTC price falls, the LTV rises.
    Margin call
    A warning from the lender that your LTV has risen to a set level. Depending on the lender, you must top up or repay part of the loan within some hours, or the lender sells part of your BTC.
    Liquidation
    The lender sells your pledged BTC to repay the loan, without asking you. It happens when the LTV reaches the liquidation level, or when a margin call is not fixed in time.
    Partial liquidation
    The lender sells only part of your BTC, enough to bring the LTV back to a lower level. The loan continues, with less BTC behind it.
    Collateral
    Something you give as security for a loan. Here: your BTC. You get it back when the loan is repaid.
    Time to top up (cure period)
    The time you have after a margin call to top up or repay part of the loan. Contracts often call it the cure period.
    Origination fee
    A one-off fee for opening the loan. It can be taken from the money you receive.
    APR vs. interest rate
    The interest rate is the price of borrowing before fees. The effective APR adds fees and the timing of payments, as one yearly percentage.
    Compounding
    Interest that is added to the debt also earns interest. The debt grows a little faster.
    Day count
    The rule for turning a yearly rate into interest for a period: each month as one twelfth of a year, or the actual days.
    Drawdown
    How far a price falls from an earlier high. From €60,000 down to €30,000 is a drawdown of 50%.
    OHLC (candle)
    Four prices for a period such as one hour: open, high, low, close. This page uses the low of every hour to check for sales.
    Price index
    The price source a lender uses to value your BTC: one exchange, or an average of several. It decides when a margin call or sale happens.
    Counterparty risk
    The risk that the other side, here the lender, does not keep its promise, for example because it goes bankrupt.
    Rehypothecation
    The lender lends out or reuses the BTC you pledged. If the lender gets into trouble, your BTC may be gone.
    Simulated price path
    One possible path of the BTC price over your loan, built from real past price moves. Counting what happens in many of them gives a chance in "N of 100".
    Block bootstrap
    The method behind the simulated price paths: pieces of real price history (30 days each) are picked at random and joined together.
    GARCH model
    A statistics model for prices in which wild days make further wild days more likely, and very large moves happen more often than in the textbook model.
    Historical replay
    The loan is started on every past day and checked against what the price really did afterwards.
    Cost of the risk
    What a liquidation takes from you by the end of the loan, on average over the simulated price paths: the missed rise on the BTC sold, and the fee. An option price, not a fee.
    Price trend
    An assumed yearly price change of the middle simulated price path (compounded). It shifts all simulated price paths up or down; the swings stay the same.

    1. Controller

    Responsible for data processing on this page: Lennart Bodden, c/o Online-Impressum 11950, Europaring 90, 53757 Sankt Augustin, Germany, e-mail: bitcoinloancheck@gmail.com.

    No data protection officer is appointed, because there is no obligation to do so.

    2. In brief

    This page has no user accounts, sets no cookies and uses no analytics, tracking or advertising services. All calculations run in your browser; your inputs are not sent to anyone.

    Personal data arise only because your browser contacts servers: the hosting service Cloudflare, which delivers the page, and a public price service for the current BTC price. Both see your IP address.

    You are not obliged to provide any data. Without your IP address, however, the page cannot be delivered to you.

    3. Delivery of the page by Cloudflare

    The page is delivered through Cloudflare Pages, including name resolution (DNS) and a worldwide delivery network. The provider is Cloudflare, Inc., 101 Townsend St., San Francisco, CA 94107, USA.

    When you open the page, Cloudflare processes the technical data that delivering any web page requires: your IP address, date and time, the address requested, your browser type and operating system. Cloudflare also uses these data to fend off attacks and may keep them in logs for a short time for that purpose.

    We ourselves only see summary figures, for example the number of visits per day and country, no IP addresses.

    Cloudflare processes the data on our behalf under its data processing agreement (Art. 28 GDPR). Cloudflare is certified under the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework, so an adequacy decision of the EU Commission applies to the USA (Art. 45 GDPR). The agreement also contains the EU standard contractual clauses.

    Legal basis: Art. 6 (1) (f) GDPR. Our legitimate interest is a secure, fast and reliable delivery of the page. More information: https://www.cloudflare.com/privacypolicy/

    4. Current BTC price

    So that the results use today's price, your browser asks Bitstamp (www.bitstamp.net) for the current BTC price when the page opens. Bitstamp has its European companies in Luxembourg.

    Only if Bitstamp does not answer, your browser asks Coinbase instead (api.coinbase.com, Coinbase, Inc., USA). Coinbase states that it is certified under the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework. Changing the currency or "Reload price" repeats the request.

    The price service receives your IP address, the time and your browser type, as with any visit to a web page. The requests contain no cookies, no referrer and nothing you entered. We receive none of these data. The price services are responsible for their own processing; details are in their privacy notices.

    Legal basis: Art. 6 (1) (f) GDPR. Our legitimate interest is calculating with a current price; without it, the results would be out of date. You can enter your own price instead.

    5. Storage in your browser

    The page stores only on your device and only what the functions you use need. These data never leave your device.

    Your inputs are kept in this browser tab's storage (session storage), so that they survive a reload; closing the tab deletes them. Only if you tick "Remember my inputs in this browser for my next visit" are they kept in your browser's local storage, until you remove the tick.

    If you choose a language or the light or dark mode, the page remembers that choice in local storage.

    "Start over and forget my inputs" removes all of these data; you can also delete them in your browser's settings.

    Legal basis: § 25 (2) No. 2 TDDDG, because the storage is strictly necessary for the function you explicitly asked for.

    6. Shared links

    If you use "Share", your inputs are written into the link after the "#" sign. Browsers do not send this part to any server, not even to Cloudflare. Whoever receives the link from you can see your inputs. On a phone, "Share" opens your device's share menu; what happens next is decided by you and the app you choose.

    7. Feedback and contact by e-mail

    "Help improve this page" and "Your language is missing?" prepare an e-mail in your own mail program. Nothing is sent unless you send it yourself. Your loan terms are attached only if you tick that box.

    If you send an e-mail, we receive your e-mail address and your message. The mailbox is run by Google Ireland Limited, Gordon House, Barrow Street, Dublin 4, Ireland. Google may also process the data in the USA.

    Google LLC is certified under the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework, so an adequacy decision of the EU Commission applies to the USA (Art. 45 GDPR).

    To sort and answer e-mails, we have new messages summarised once a day by the AI service Claude. Claude is provided by Anthropic Ireland, Limited, 6th Floor, South Bank House, Barrow Street, Dublin 4, D04 TR29, Ireland. Anthropic also processes the data in the USA, under EU standard contractual clauses (Art. 46 GDPR). Claude only reads: it sends, answers and deletes nothing. We have switched off the use of our conversations for training AI models.

    We use your message only to read it, answer it and improve the page, and delete it once it is no longer needed for that, at the latest after twelve months. Legal basis: Art. 6 (1) (f) GDPR; our legitimate interest is answering you and improving the page.

    11. Your rights

    You have the right of access (Art. 15 GDPR), rectification (Art. 16), erasure (Art. 17), restriction of processing (Art. 18) and data portability (Art. 20).
